Elevators can have weight sensors. It's not a new thing. As long as nobody needs to carry along a whole extra person's worth of heavy equipment, the elevator can be programmed to have some level of tolerance which would allow people to bring stuff in the elevator along with them. Here's how it works: you get on, the elevator measures the total weight of you and whatever you brought with you, and then you place your cargo in the corner of the elevator where it is weighed separately. This separate weight is subtracted to arrive at your own weight. A camera takes a picture of you and your cargo and matches your weight up to the weight associated with your ID card. The picture also serves as a record to ensure you're not giving anyone free rides. Cameras in elevators are not a new thing.

Finally an article on automation that actually tells it like it is. Robots have been in industry for a long time now. They haven't replaced human workers across the board because they aren't as adaptable as humans. Getting them to do a single job or maybe a few similar jobs is expensive and time consuming. it is also not a guarantee they will work flawlessly. When a job changes, say a new product is to be made, the whole automation system might need to change. That's more time, expense and effort than simply training people to do the new job. But even if you are willing to pay the price and stay the robot course, what happens when a robot cannot adapt to an unexpected event? What if a manufacturing defect in a part or assembly causes issues? What if a robot upstream on the line is malfunctioning and making bad parts? What if a robot outright fails and there is no backup for that robot's job? There are many problems that humans can work around quickly and avoid downtime and costly rework or waste.

Oh, but I forget. AI is the answer. Yeah, AI will make all these potential problems disappear because they can learn and adapt. AI will be better than a human in fact since they can think faster, better and more abstractly than any human. Sure. Yeah, that's it. Sigh. AI will have the same kinds of limitations humans will if that is the case. An AI might be able to come up with a solution, but with its physical limitations, how many of those solutions could it actually put to use? Will it be able to avoid paradoxes that rob Peter to pay Paul on the assembly line? Can it keep from destroying the production line if it makes bad choices? Who watches it and makes sure these things don't happen? Yeah, AI and robots are not going to make humans obsolete any time soon. And they will never be more cost effective than wage slaves. It's a pipe dream for the foreseeable future. It's just another scare tactic used by people who know nothing about the process or technology. We'll sooner see the end of the FAX machine and the truly paperless offices that have been touted for nearly as long.

The biggest thing this article ignores is that all of the extras (pedestal, end effectors, workpiece holding arrangement etc.) have equivalents in a manned factory (your workers aren't lifting that 600kg car chassis by themselves, and welding it together by pointing a finger and saying "pew pew"!) which also cost significant amounts of money. For a retrofit, maybe you just throw that stuff out, but for a new factory, the marginal cost of automation is still low compared with the cost of workers.

Also, remember that:

  • Replacing "one worker" saves you 3x - 4x their salary when you take into account that workers only work 8-12hrs/day and don't work weekends/holidays
  • Workers are human and screw up occasionally, leading to extra costs/delays
  • Sometimes those screwups result in injuries, workers comp claims or extended time off
  • Workers quit and need to be replaced/retrained, and you need extra staff to do the hiring and training
  • You may need fewer production lines because machines tend to be faster and don't screw up or have lapses of concentration

Basically, unless you're doing short run production, the extra setup cost for robots is trivial because it's amortized over huge numbers of units produced.

In certain industries trust is also important.

For example in logistics you have to worry about employees stealing cargo. What better way to prevent theft then remove humans from the environment?

You can also program them to not sexually harass people, where's the fun in that though? Plenty of lawsuits in general can be avoided by using robots over humans.
